decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: Where must you stop at a stop sign?
cards.back: At a stop sign you must stop completely, before the stop line if one is marked, or before the crosswalk if there is one.

cards.front: What must you do after stopping at a stop sign?
cards.back: After stopping at a stop sign, yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and traffic before you go, and if your view of the intersection is blocked, be ready to stop again.

cards.front: Where must you stop before entering a road from an alley, driveway or lot?
cards.back: Stop completely before pulling onto a road from an alley, a private driveway, a parking lot or a parking ramp, and always stop before driving across a sidewalk or crosswalk.

cards.front: What must you do at a red traffic signal?
cards.back: At a red traffic signal, stop and wait until the light is green and your path is clear before going.

cards.front: How does a steady red light differ from a flashing red light?
cards.back: A steady red signal means stop and wait for green, while a flashing red light means stop and then go when clear, just as at a stop sign.

cards.front: How do you treat a flashing red traffic light?
cards.back: Treat a flashing red traffic light exactly like a stop sign.
cards.memory_hook: Flashing red is a stop sign

cards.front: When must you stop at a crosswalk for a pedestrian or bicyclist?
cards.back: Stop at any crosswalk, marked or unmarked, where a pedestrian or bicyclist is crossing, and stay stopped until they have passed your lane.

cards.front: Which other signals and situations require a full stop?
cards.back: Full stops are also required for a red freeway ramp meter, for a railroad crossing posted with a stop sign, when a flag person or traffic device signals you to halt, and at a bridge raised for boats.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: How far before stopping does a school bus turn on yellow lights in slower zones?
cards.back: In a speed zone of thirty-five miles per hour or less, a school bus driver turns on the flashing yellow lights at least one hundred feet before the bus stops.

cards.front: How far before stopping does a school bus turn on yellow lights in faster zones?
cards.back: In a speed zone above thirty-five miles per hour, a school bus driver turns on the flashing yellow lights at least three hundred feet before the bus stops.

cards.front: How far ahead of a stop do school bus flashing yellow lights activate by speed zone?
cards.back: School buses flash yellow and red lights alternately when stopping for students, activating flashing yellow lights at least one hundred feet ahead in speed zones of thirty-five miles per hour or less and at least three hundred feet ahead in faster zones.
cards.memory_hook: Minimum one hundred or three hundred

cards.front: May you pass a school bus on its right while its lights flash?
cards.back: Passing a school bus on its right side while it shows flashing red or yellow lights is against the law.

cards.front: How far from a stopped school bus with flashing red lights must you stop?
cards.back: When a stopped school bus has its red lights flashing, you must stop at least twenty feet away from it.

cards.front: How long must you stay stopped for a school bus?
cards.back: Whether you are facing the front or the back of the bus, you stay stopped until its red lights stop flashing.

cards.front: What is the penalty for failing to stop for a school bus?
cards.back: Failing to stop for a school bus is a misdemeanor, and a conviction brings a fine of at least five hundred dollars and the loss of your driving privileges.

cards.front: When do you not have to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights?
cards.back: On a divided roadway you do not have to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights that is on the other side of the divider.

cards.front: Without a divider, which drivers must stop for a school bus?
cards.back: Without a divider, the duty to stop for a bus with flashing red lights covers traffic from both directions, behind the bus and facing it; only a divided roadway frees drivers on the far side.

cards.front: How long after an illegal school bus pass may an officer arrest you?
cards.back: An officer with probable cause to believe you illegally passed a stopped school bus may arrest you within four hours of the violation.

cards.front: What happens to the owner of a vehicle used to break the school bus law?
cards.back: The owner or lessee of a vehicle used to break the school bus stopping law is guilty of a petty misdemeanor unless they can prove someone else was driving, in which case the driver is charged.

cards.front: How do the penalties differ for the driver and the owner in a school bus violation?
cards.back: A driver who passes a stopped school bus faces a misdemeanor, while the vehicle's owner or lessee faces a petty misdemeanor unless they show someone else was driving.

cards.front: What do you certify about school buses on a license application?
cards.back: When you sign a driver's license application, you certify that you understand the duty to stop for a school bus and know the penalties for breaking that law.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: Who must you stop for at school crossings?
cards.back: Come to a complete stop for a student safety patrol helping classmates cross, and for an adult crossing guard holding a stop sign or flag.

cards.front: Is it legal to drive through a line of children crossing when no patrol is present?
cards.back: Driving through a line of children crossing the road is illegal even with no safety patrol present; it is a misdemeanor, and a second violation within a year is a gross misdemeanor.

cards.front: What must you do for a school bus flagger?
cards.back: Stop for a school bus flagger who is holding traffic so buses can leave school property, and do not move on until the flagger or a police officer tells you to.

cards.front: What are right-of-way laws based on, and why do they matter?
cards.back: Right-of-way and yielding laws rest on courtesy and common sense, and breaking them is a leading cause of traffic crashes.

cards.front: Two drivers reach an uncontrolled or all-way stop intersection together. Who yields?
cards.back: At an intersection without signals, and at an all-way stop or flashing red light, when two drivers arrive together the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.

cards.front: Whom must you yield to when turning left?
cards.back: When turning left, yield to oncoming vehicles that are in the intersection or near enough to cause a crash.

cards.front: Does a green left arrow mean you never need to yield?
cards.back: A green left-turn arrow still requires you to yield to vehicles or pedestrians already in the intersection before you continue in the arrow's direction.

cards.front: Who yields at an uncontrolled T intersection?
cards.back: At an uncontrolled T intersection, the driver who is turning yields to all cross traffic.

cards.front: Which buses must a right-lane driver yield to?
cards.back: A driver in the right-hand lane yields to transit and metro mobility buses merging out of a bus stop or off the shoulder, and to a school bus re-entering the lane after loading, which shows its left turn signal.

cards.front: When must you yield to a funeral procession?
cards.back: Yield to every vehicle in a funeral procession once it marks itself with headlights or hazard warning lights.

cards.front: What must you do when entering a public road from a driveway, and at crosswalks?
cards.back: Coming out of a private road or driveway onto a public road, you stop and yield to pedestrians and traffic, and at intersections and crosswalks, marked or unmarked, you always yield to crossing pedestrians.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: What must you do when an emergency vehicle with lights and siren approaches?
cards.back: When an emergency vehicle with flashing red lights and a siren or bell comes toward you on a two-way road, move right and stop; on a one-way road move to the closer side; finish crossing an intersection first if you are in one; and stay stopped until every emergency vehicle has gone by.

cards.front: When need you not stop for an approaching emergency vehicle?
cards.back: You need not stop for an emergency vehicle that is separated from your lane by a physical barrier such as a fence, wall or median strip.

cards.front: How long after failing to yield to an emergency vehicle may an officer arrest you?
cards.back: An officer with probable cause to believe you failed to yield to an emergency vehicle may arrest you within four hours of the violation.

cards.front: What does the Move Over Law require on a road with two lanes your way?
cards.back: Under the Move Over Law, when an emergency vehicle with flashing lights is stopped on or beside a road with two lanes in your direction, move to the lane farthest from it if it is safe; tow trucks count as emergency vehicles.

cards.front: Which other vehicles does the Move Over rule cover?
cards.back: The Move Over rule also applies to stalled or disabled vehicles and to stopped service patrol, road maintenance, utility, construction, postal, and solid waste or recycling vehicles with warning lights on.

cards.front: What if you cannot move over a lane for a stopped emergency vehicle?
cards.back: If you cannot move over a lane, or the road has only one lane in your direction, slow down and pass the stopped vehicle with caution.

cards.front: How close may you follow a firefighting vehicle on an emergency run?
cards.back: Only vehicles on official emergency business may follow within five hundred feet of a firefighting vehicle on an emergency run.

cards.front: May you drive over an unprotected fire hose?
cards.back: Never drive over an unprotected fire hose unless a law enforcement officer or fire department official tells you to.

cards.front: How should you set your following distance?
cards.back: Keep enough distance behind the vehicle ahead to stop or turn away from a collision, adjust it for weather, traffic and road conditions, and use the three-second rule taught later in the manual.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: How do careless driving and reckless driving differ?
cards.back: Careless driving endangers people or property, while reckless driving means knowingly ignoring a substantial and unjustifiable risk to others, which includes racing whether or not the speed limit is exceeded.

cards.front: How is a careless or reckless driving charge tried?
cards.back: A charge of either careless or reckless driving is tried in court as a misdemeanor.

cards.front: What should you do when emergency lights appear behind you?
cards.back: When emergency lights appear behind you, stay calm, slow down, signal and pull onto the right shoulder as soon as it is safe, avoiding bridges, curves and the traffic lane.

cards.front: When may you pull onto the left shoulder for police?
cards.back: On a multi-lane road, if you are nearer the left shoulder and it has room for a full lane, you may pull over onto the left shoulder instead of the right.

cards.front: What should you do during a traffic stop after dark?
cards.back: During a stop after dark, switch on the interior light, keep the doors shut, stay inside unless the officer says otherwise, and keep your hands visible on the steering wheel.

cards.front: What should you do if your documents are out of reach during a stop?
cards.back: If your license or insurance proof is out of reach, tell the officer where it is before reaching, and do not get out of the vehicle or approach the officer unless you ask and are given permission.

cards.front: What should you do if you have a firearm in the vehicle during a stop?
cards.back: With a firearm in the vehicle, leave both hands visible on the wheel, tell the officer about the firearm and its location as soon as they approach, and never reach for it.

cards.front: What should you do if you disagree with a citation?
cards.back: If you disagree with a citation, do not argue at the roadside; explain your view in court, and ask any questions before the officer finishes the stop.

cards.front: What happens if you disobey a lawful order from an officer?
cards.back: Not obeying a lawful order or direction from an officer is illegal and can lead to arrest, and you should not resist if taken into custody.

cards.front: What is traffic enforcement meant to achieve?
cards.back: Traffic enforcement aims to change unsafe behavior, reduce crashes and injuries and save lives, and a warning or citation is meant to deter future unsafe driving.

decks.domain: Sharing the road confusables and continuation facts

cards.front: What will an officer usually do during a traffic stop?
cards.back: During a stop the officer will usually greet you, say they are a law enforcement officer, ask for your license and insurance proof, explain the reason for the stop and check that your license is valid.

cards.front: Which forms of identification are accepted at a traffic stop?
cards.back: Identification accepted at a traffic stop includes a Minnesota or out-of-state driver's license, a temporary license, a learner's permit, a military ID, and a consulate or international driver's license.

cards.front: Does accepting a citation mean you admit guilt?
cards.back: Accepting a citation is not an admission of guilt; it only acknowledges that you received it and promises that you will appear in court if required.

cards.front: Where do citations go, and what option may the court offer?
cards.back: Citations go to a local jurisdiction for a hearing, and the court may offer a diversion program such as driver education training.

cards.front: Where do you send concerns about an officer's conduct?
cards.back: Concerns about an officer's conduct go to the officer's agency or supervisor, using the officer information printed on the citation.

cards.front: What is the penalty for fleeing a police officer in a vehicle?
cards.back: Fleeing a police officer in a motor vehicle is a felony punishable by up to three years and one day in prison, a fine of up to five thousand dollars, or both.

cards.front: How do fleeing penalties rise when someone is hurt or killed?
cards.back: If someone dies because a driver fled police, the penalty reaches up to ten years in prison and a twenty thousand dollars fine; great bodily harm brings up to seven years and fourteen thousand dollars; substantial bodily harm brings up to five years and ten thousand dollars.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: May you pass a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian?
cards.back: Passing a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian is illegal, so when another vehicle stops, look for someone in the crosswalk and be ready to stop.

cards.front: How should you treat a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog?
cards.back: Watch for blind pedestrians carrying a white or metallic cane or using a guide dog, and do not honk or rev the engine near them.

cards.front: How do marked and unmarked crosswalks differ?
cards.back: A marked crosswalk has solid white lines and may have signs or flashing lights, while an unmarked crosswalk is where a sidewalk meets the road with no lines painted.
cards.memory_hook: Lines or no lines, still crosswalks

cards.front: What is the penalty for breaking pedestrian right-of-way laws?
cards.back: Breaking pedestrian right-of-way laws is a misdemeanor, and a second violation within a year becomes a gross misdemeanor.

cards.front: Where should you watch extra carefully for pedestrians?
cards.back: Watch extra carefully for pedestrians on streets lined with parked cars, in poor visibility and wherever children are around, and never stop with your vehicle blocking a crosswalk.

cards.front: What should pedestrians do at signals?
cards.back: Pedestrians should obey signals, wait a few feet back from the road for the WALK signal, still yield to vehicles already in the intersection, and make eye contact so drivers yield before they cross.

cards.front: What should a pedestrian do where there is no crosswalk?
cards.back: Where there is no crosswalk a pedestrian yields to all vehicles, and if walking on the road is necessary, walks on the left side facing oncoming traffic.

cards.front: How can pedestrians be seen at night?
cards.back: At night or in poor visibility, pedestrians should wear light-colored clothing with reflective material or carry a flashlight, and expect that sun glare may keep drivers from seeing them.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: stopping, school buses, right-of-way, emergency vehicles, traffic stops, pedestrians and bicyclists

cards.front: Are bicycles legal vehicles on Minnesota roads?
cards.back: Bicycles are legal vehicles on Minnesota roads with the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicles.

cards.front: When may you drive in a bicycle lane?
cards.back: Driving in a bicycle lane is illegal except to park where allowed, to enter or leave the road, or to prepare for a turn, and you must yield to approaching bicyclists before moving into it.
cards.memory_hook: Bike lane only to park, turn

cards.front: How do you turn across a bicycle lane?
cards.back: Before turning across a bicycle lane, make sure it is clear, signal, and move into the bicycle lane before you make the turn.

cards.front: How much space must you leave when passing a bicyclist?
cards.back: When passing a bicyclist, leave at least three feet between the side of your car and the rider.

cards.front: May you cross the center line to pass a bicyclist in a no passing zone?
cards.back: When it is safe, you may cross the center of the road to pass a bicyclist even in a no passing zone, after making sure the rider is not signaling or turning left.

cards.front: How are electric-assist bicycles and mopeds treated?
cards.back: Electric-assist bicycles follow the same road rules as bicycles, while mopeds, which have a gas engine, follow different rules.

cards.front: Which traffic rules must bicyclists follow?
cards.back: Bicyclists must obey all traffic laws, ride with the flow of traffic, signal every turn and obey traffic control signs, signals and devices.

cards.front: What must a bicyclist do at a stop sign?
cards.back: At a stop sign a bicyclist must slow enough to be able to stop before the intersection or crosswalk, and may continue without stopping when no vehicle is nearby.

cards.front: Where in the lane do bicyclists ride?
cards.back: Bicyclists ride just to the right of faster traffic but may move toward the center of the lane for hazards, when passing or when turning left.

cards.front: Which hand signals do bicyclists use for right turns and stopping?
cards.back: A bicyclist signals a right turn with the left arm bent upward or the right arm held straight out, and signals stopping with the left arm bent down toward the ground.
cards.memory_hook: Arm up right, arm down stop

cards.front: May bicyclists ride side by side?
cards.back: Two bicyclists may ride side by side if they stay within one lane and do not impede traffic, and riders should wear helmets for safety.

cards.front: What lights and tires may a bicycle use at night?
cards.back: At night a bicycle needs legal lights and reflectors and may use a white flashing front lamp, a red flashing rear lamp or both, and tires with spikes are allowed for traction.

cards.front: What rules apply to bicyclists on sidewalks?
cards.back: On sidewalks and crosswalks a bicyclist yields to pedestrians, gives an audible signal before passing them, has a pedestrian's rights and duties, and may not ride on business district sidewalks unless local authorities allow it.

recap_hooks.text: Stop fully at stop signs, before driveways meet the road, at red lights and wherever someone is crossing.
Treat a flashing red light like a stop sign, and stop for ramp meters, rail stop signs, flaggers and raised bridges.
School bus yellow lights start one hundred feet before a stop in slower zones and three hundred in faster ones.
Stop at least twenty feet from a bus with flashing red lights and stay stopped, unless a divider puts you on the far side.
Stop for patrols, crossing guards and flaggers, and never drive through children crossing.
At uncontrolled or all-way intersections the left driver yields to the right, and at a T the turning driver yields.
Pull right and stop for an approaching emergency vehicle unless a barrier separates you, and move over a lane for stopped ones.
Stay five hundred feet behind a firefighting vehicle on a run.
When an officer signals you, pull over safely, keep your hands visible and stay in the vehicle.
Tell the officer about any firearm right away, and argue a citation in court, not at the roadside.
Accepting a citation is not admitting guilt, and fleeing police is a felony with harsher penalties if anyone is hurt.
Never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, and stay quiet around blind pedestrians.
Crosswalks may be marked or unmarked, and pedestrians on roads without sidewalks walk facing traffic.
Bicycles are legal vehicles, so give them at least three feet when passing and stay out of bike lanes except to park or turn.
Bicyclists ride with traffic, signal turns and obey traffic controls.
